cases.holding: The court held that a CHINS adjudication establishes the status of the child and need not be entered separately as to each parent, but it vacated the dispositional decree as to N.E. because the juvenile court failed to state why the child was not placed with his father as the least restrictive placement.
cases.quote: Because a CHINS proceeding is a civil action, the State must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that a child is a CHINS as defined by the juvenile code.

relevance.DEC-03: Fixes the preponderance standard and the statutory elements the agency must prove before a child is found in need of services.
relevance.ACT-03: Requires the dispositional decree to explain why a less restrictive, family-like placement was rejected before the child is placed in foster care.
relevance.ACT-04: Holds the court must articulate reasons for not placing the child with the non-offending parent, the starting point for kinship-placement analysis.
relevance.ACT-05: Shows that dispositional orders restricting a parent must be supported by stated reasons tied to the statutory least-restrictive mandate.

cases.holding: The court reversed the CHINS adjudication, holding the evidence did not show the mother was unlikely to meet the children's needs without the coercive intervention of the court, and it declined to find the appeal moot because of the collateral consequences of a CHINS judgment.
cases.quote: The intrusion of a CHINS judgment, then, must be reserved for families who cannot meet those needs without coercion

relevance.INP-05: Confirms that a family that seeks and accepts help voluntarily is not a proper subject of a coercive CHINS case.
relevance.INP-10: Sets the limit on escalating an assessment into a court case: need for coercion, not merely difficulty, is the trigger.
relevance.DEC-01: Supplies the legal basis for closing or declining a case where the family will accept services without court compulsion.
relevance.DEC-03: Explains that endangerment alone does not justify a founded CHINS finding absent proof coercion is required.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports a differential/alternative response where services can be delivered without a petition.
relevance.ACT-01: Directly supports voluntary service plans as the preferred route when the family is cooperating.
relevance.FAIL-01: A leading example of appellate reversal of an agency-obtained CHINS adjudication for insufficient proof of the coercion element.

cases.holding: The court reversed the CHINS adjudication because the Department failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence the third statutory element, that the children needed care the parents were unlikely to provide without the court's coercive intervention.
cases.quote: To prove a child is “in need of services”, the Department must prove three statutory elements by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.INP-10: States the three elements that must be met before an intake is escalated into a court adjudication.
relevance.DEC-01: Where the third element fails, the correct outcome is no court case at all.
relevance.DEC-02: Frames what an accepted assessment must ultimately be able to prove.
relevance.DEC-03: The controlling recent statement of the elements and the preponderance burden for a founded finding.
relevance.ACT-01: Where parents voluntarily secured services, coercive intervention was not shown and voluntary services were the correct response.
relevance.OUT-01: Reversal returned the children to the parents, illustrating the evidentiary floor for continued state involvement.
relevance.OUT-05: Failure of proof on any element requires dismissal of the CHINS petition.
relevance.FAIL-01: Leading modern reversal of a CHINS adjudication by the state's highest court.

cases.holding: The court held that a parent who requests a contested fact-finding hearing in a CHINS case has a procedural due process right to that hearing, and that in fact-sensitive situations due process requires separate fact findings as to each parent.
cases.quote: We hold that a parent who requests a contested fact-finding hearing has a due process right to that hearing.

relevance.INP-04: Judicially initiated or continued CHINS involvement still requires the contested hearing a parent requests.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated allegation may not be converted into an adjudication without the contested fact-finding hearing a parent demands.
relevance.DEC-05: Once a petition is filed, the parent's request for a contested fact-finding hearing must be honored before disposition.
relevance.ACT-05: Court-imposed dispositional restraints cannot rest on a disposition hearing substituted for the fact-finding hearing a parent requested.

cases.holding: The court held that the claim-preclusion branch of res judicata applies to CHINS proceedings, condemning repetitive filings, but affirmed because the parents did not raise the defense and the trial court had no duty to raise it sua sponte.
cases.quote: We hold today that the claim preclusion branch of res judicata applies to CHINS proceedings.

relevance.DEC-05: Limits the agency's ability to re-file successive CHINS petitions on the same facts after an earlier petition failed.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination of the father's parental rights, deferring to the trial court's weighing of his late progress against his history of violence and the children's need for permanency after years in out-of-home care.
cases.quote: Simply stated, children cannot wait indefinitely for their parents to work toward preservation or reunification

relevance.OUT-02: The leading modern Indiana statement of appellate deference on the remedy-of-conditions and best-interests elements of termination.

cases.holding: The court held that because DCS failed to prove the statutory waiting-period element it alleged, the trial court was required to dismiss the termination petitions, and it reversed the terminations.
cases.quote: requiring a termination petition to allege four defined elements and commanding dismissal when DCS fails to prove each element by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: Establishes that every statutory element of termination, including the waiting period, must be pleaded and proved by clear and convincing evidence or the petition must be dismissed.

cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights, holding the evidence was insufficient where he had completed numerous programs in prison, maintained regular contact, and the child was placed with a suitable relative.
cases.quote: We hold that there was insufficient evidence to terminate Father's parental rights to K.E., and we reverse the trial court's order terminating Father's parental rights.

relevance.ACT-04: Treats placement of the child with a paternal aunt as a suitable arrangement weighing against termination, supporting kinship placement.
relevance.OUT-02: Controlling Indiana authority that incarceration alone, where the parent pursues services and maintains contact, does not support termination.

cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of an incarcerated mother's parental rights, concluding the evidence did not clearly and convincingly show that the conditions leading to removal would not be remedied or that termination was in the child's best interests where she maintained consistent visitation and pursued available prison programming.
cases.quote: The State's burden of proof in termination of parental rights cases is one of “clear and convincing evidence.”

relevance.FAIL-01: A leading reversal by the state's highest court of a termination judgment obtained on an insufficient record against an incarcerated parent.

cases.holding: The court held that the statutory right to counsel in a termination case continues through all stages including appeal, but affirmed the refusal to appoint appellate counsel here because trial counsel had no basis on which to file an appeal.
cases.quote: We hold that our statutes dictate that the right to counsel continues through all stages of the proceeding to terminate the parent-child relationship, including appeal.

relevance.OUT-02: Establishes that an indigent parent's right to counsel in Indiana termination proceedings extends through the appeal from the termination order.

cases.holding: The court vacated the judgment terminating the mother's parental rights because the CHINS court found her indigent and entitled to counsel but never appointed one, and those defective CHINS proceedings flowed directly into the termination action.
cases.quote: J.A. was denied her statutory right to counsel during the course of the CHINS proceedings below and those proceedings flowed directly into an action to terminate her parental rights

relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered service plans entered without the counsel a parent was found entitled to cannot support later termination.
relevance.OUT-01: Denial of counsel during the reunification phase of a CHINS case is a due process defect that infects the whole case.
relevance.FAIL-01: Leading Indiana authority vacating a termination judgment for procedural irregularities occurring in the underlying CHINS case.

cases.case_name: Baker v. Marion County Office of Family & Children
cases.holding: The court adopted a fundamental-fairness standard, rather than the criminal Strickland test, for claims that counsel underperformed in a termination case, and affirmed because joint representation of both parents did not render the hearing fundamentally unfair.
cases.quote: we deem the focus of the inquiry to be whether it appears that the parents received a fundamentally fair trial whose facts demonstrate an accurate determination

relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the Indiana standard for attacking a termination judgment on the ground that appointed counsel performed inadequately.

cases.case_name: Indiana Department of Child Services v. A.B.
cases.holding: The court upheld the juvenile court's out-of-state residential placement over the agency's objection, held the agency's insistence on an in-state placement arbitrary and capricious, and ordered DCS to pay for the placement.
cases.quote: Finally, we hold that DCS shall pay for the placement of the child at Canyon State Academy.

relevance.INP-04: Confirms the juvenile court's authority to direct the agency's involvement and placement notwithstanding the agency's contrary position.
relevance.ACT-02: Establishes that the court, not the agency, controls the services and placement ordered in the dispositional decree, and that the agency must fund them.
relevance.ACT-03: Governs who decides and who pays when the court and DCS disagree about a child's out-of-home placement.
relevance.OUT-01: Placement and funding disputes cannot be used by the agency to override the court's judgment about what the child needs.
relevance.OUT-04: Applied to an older youth's residential placement and the agency's continuing duty to fund court-ordered care.
relevance.PMC-02: Shows judicial review of agency financial decisions about child-welfare placements under Indiana administrative-review standards.

cases.holding: The court held that a third party seeking custody or guardianship over a natural parent must overcome a strong presumption favoring the parent by clear and convincing evidence that placement with the third party is a substantial and significant advantage to the child.
cases.quote: The trial court must be convinced that placement with a person other than the natural parent represents a substantial and significant advantage to the child.

relevance.ACT-04: Sets the evidentiary bar a relative or other caregiver must clear to obtain custody over a parent's objection.
relevance.OUT-03: The controlling Indiana standard for awarding guardianship of a child to someone other than the natural parent.

cases.holding: The court held that an untimely notice of appeal forfeits but does not extinguish the right to appeal, and restored the father's forfeited appeal from an adoption decree because extraordinarily compelling reasons, including the constitutional weight of parental rights, were present.
cases.quote: the right to appeal having been forfeited, the question is whether there are extraordinarily compelling reasons why this forfeited right should be restored

relevance.OUT-03: Governs appellate access for a parent contesting an adoption or permanency order entered without consent.
relevance.FAIL-01: Provides the route by which a parent whose lawyer missed the appeal deadline can still obtain appellate review of a permanency order.

cases.case_name: D.S. v. County Department of Public Welfare of St. Joseph County
cases.holding: The court reversed a termination of parental rights because the trial court failed to comply with the Indian Child Welfare Act on both transfer of jurisdiction and the Act's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt evidentiary standard supported by qualified expert testimony, and it rejected the 'existing Indian family' limitation.
cases.quote: the trial court did not follow the provisions of the ICWA as they relate to jurisdiction and the evidentiary standard to be applied in terminating parental rights, we must reverse

relevance.INP-11: The controlling Indiana Supreme Court decision on when ICWA's jurisdictional and evidentiary requirements attach to a state child-welfare case.

cases.case_name: John Doe #1 v. Indiana Department of Child Services
cases.holding: The court held that the statute requiring DCS to protect a child-abuse reporter's identity creates no private right of action and that the hotline operator's assurance of anonymity created no common-law duty, so the reporter's family had no remedy when DCS released his unredacted report.
cases.quote: We denounce DCS's thoughtlessness, but find no basis for liability under either theory.

relevance.INP-01: Tells mandated reporters that the statutory promise of confidentiality is not privately enforceable if the agency breaches it.
relevance.INP-02: Defines the practical limit of confidentiality protection for any citizen who makes a report.
relevance.INP-06: Directly addresses the anonymity a hotline operator promises and holds it unenforceable in damages.
relevance.FAIL-06: Shows that an agency's improper disclosure of protected records carries no private damages remedy under Indiana law.
relevance.PMC-05: Marks the boundary between records the agency must protect and the remedies available when it fails to.

cases.holding: The court reversed dismissal of a malpractice suit against a physician who reported suspected medical child abuse to DCS, holding Indiana's anti-SLAPP statute did not apply because the suit targeted her medical care rather than speech on a public issue.
cases.quote: a person's actions must be “in furtherance of” his or her right of petition or free speech and “in connection with a public issue.”

relevance.INP-01: Shows that the anti-SLAPP statute is not a shield for a mandated reporter sued over the care surrounding the report.
relevance.INP-02: Clarifies which protections do and do not attach to a person who reports suspected abuse.
relevance.INP-06: Defines the limits of speech-based protection for reports routed to the child-abuse hotline.
relevance.INP-07: Arises directly from a physician's report of suspected medical child abuse made during a hospital admission.
relevance.INP-08: Illustrates the scope of protection for professionals who report suspected abuse observed in their institutional role.
relevance.ACT-06: Concerns the consequences of a medical provider's abuse report made in the course of emergency pediatric care.
relevance.FAIL-05: Defines when a lawsuit against a reporter is and is not an actionable retaliatory SLAPP under Indiana law.

cases.case_name: Indiana Department of Child Services v. LaPorte Circuit Court
cases.holding: The court held that expedited Appellate Rule 14.1 review is available when a juvenile court rejects a DCS placement recommendation, that the court must accept the recommendation unless it finds by a preponderance that the recommendation is unreasonable or contrary to the child's welfare and best interests, and that such a finding is reviewed for clear error.
cases.quote: a finding by the juvenile court that DCS's recommendation is unreasonable or contrary to the child's welfare and best interests is reviewed on appeal for clear error

relevance.INP-04: Defines the division of authority between the juvenile court and DCS once the court is involved in a child's case.
relevance.INP-09: Creates the expedited appellate mechanism through which placement decisions are externally reviewed.
relevance.ACT-03: Governs when a juvenile court may reject the agency's foster-placement recommendation and how that decision is reviewed.
relevance.FAIL-03: Provides the state-law check on agency placement decisions that federal IV-E oversight assumes courts will exercise.
relevance.PMC-01: Supplies the judicial-determination mechanism that federal reviews measure when assessing state placement oversight.

cases.case_name: ESPN, Inc. v. University of Notre Dame Police Department
cases.holding: The court held that a private university's police department is not a 'public agency' subject to Indiana's Access to Public Records Act, and that APRA's liberal-construction directive governs which records are disclosable rather than which entities are covered.
cases.quote: We too find that a private university police department is not a “public agency” for the purposes of APRA, and affirm the trial court.

relevance.INP-09: Defines which entities are subject to Indiana's open-records law when oversight bodies seek child-welfare data.
relevance.FAIL-06: Sets the coverage limit of Indiana's transparency statute, which determines whether a disclosure failure is actionable at all.
relevance.PMC-02: Determines whether an audit or records request can reach a private contractor performing public-facing functions.
relevance.PMC-03: Bears on whether citizen review bodies can compel records from private entities under APRA.
relevance.PMC-05: The controlling Indiana Supreme Court authority on APRA's scope for transparency requests.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes the legal boundary of the public records any cross-jurisdictional data analysis can lawfully obtain in Indiana.

cases.holding: The court reversed an order granting the media access to two children's CHINS records, holding the juvenile court abused its discretion where there was no specific ongoing threat to the safety or welfare of the community.
cases.quote: Because there is no specific ongoing threat to the safety or welfare of the community, the trial court abused its discretion in disclosing the children's CHINS records.

relevance.OUT-06: Governs media access to CHINS records of surviving siblings after a child's death in the home.
relevance.FAIL-06: Identifies when withholding, rather than releasing, juvenile records is legally required in Indiana.
relevance.PMC-05: Sets the standard a transparency request must meet before confidential CHINS records may be opened.

cases.holding: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding among other things that the juvenile court erred in releasing records from the mother's own delinquency proceedings but did not err in releasing DCS records concerning the child under the fatality and near-fatality disclosure statute.
cases.quote: the juvenile court did not err in releasing IDCS and MCDCS records regarding T.B. pursuant to Indiana Code Section 31-33-18-1.5

relevance.OUT-06: Applies Indiana's fatality and near-fatality records-disclosure statute to agency records about the affected child.
relevance.FAIL-04: Provides the disclosure mechanism triggered when a child dies or nearly dies while known to the agency.
relevance.FAIL-06: Distinguishes records that must be released from those that remain confidential, defining what counts as a disclosure failure.
relevance.PMC-03: Shows the record set available to review bodies examining agency handling of a serious-injury case.
relevance.PMC-04: Supplies the Indiana statutory pathway for fatality-review access to agency records.
relevance.PMC-05: Applies the strongest Indiana disclosure mandate in the child-welfare records context.
relevance.PMC-06: Defines the lawfully obtainable Indiana record set for fatality and near-fatality analysis.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of the grandmother's and step-grandfather's petitions, holding that once the mother's parental rights were terminated the grandmother was no longer the child's grandparent for purposes of the relative-placement and visitation statutes.
cases.quote: We conclude that because Mother's parental rights were terminated prior to the filing of the Leonellis' petition for placement, Mrs. Leonelli was no longer G.R.'s grandparent

relevance.ACT-03: Explains when relatives lose standing to contest a foster placement made during the CHINS case.
relevance.ACT-04: Applies Indiana's relative-placement preference statute and fixes the point at which kinship status ends.
relevance.OUT-03: Governs whether a relative may seek kinship permanency after parental rights have already been terminated.

cases.case_name: B.R. ex rel. Todd v. State
cases.holding: The court reversed dismissal of a foster child's suit against the DCS-contracted mental health center, holding that claims of negligent placement and failure to warn the respite foster parents sound in general negligence and are not subject to the Medical Malpractice Act's procedural bar.
cases.quote: Because B.R.'s claims sound in general negligence, his claims fall outside the Medical Malpractice Act.

relevance.OUT-06: Preserves a civil remedy for a child seriously harmed while in an agency-arranged placement.
relevance.FAIL-04: Establishes the route by which harm to a child under agency supervision is litigated in Indiana.
relevance.PMC-04: Shows how agency and contractor conduct in a serious-injury case is examined through civil litigation.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the placement of the child with his out-of-state father and the dismissal of the CHINS case, holding DCS's reunification efforts were reasonable and did not violate the statutory reasonable-efforts provision.
cases.quote: In light of the circumstances, we believe DCS's reunification efforts were reasonable.

relevance.INP-05: Shows the agency responding to family circumstances by locating and engaging an available parent rather than escalating.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports resolving a case through placement and dismissal rather than continued court supervision.
relevance.ACT-02: Applies Indiana's statutory reasonable-efforts requirement to the services ordered during a CHINS case.
relevance.OUT-01: Treats placement with a previously absent parent as a reunification outcome satisfying reasonable efforts.
relevance.OUT-05: Upholds dismissal of the CHINS case once the child was safely placed.
relevance.FAIL-03: Applies Ind. Code 31-34-21-5.5, the state codification of the federal reasonable-efforts requirement.
relevance.PMC-01: Illustrates the state-court reasonable-efforts determination that federal CFSR review measures.

cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for the pediatrician, holding Indiana does not recognize a private right of action against a person who fails to report suspected child abuse or neglect.
cases.quote: Because Indiana does not recognize a private right of action for failure to report child abuse or neglect, we affirm the trial court's entry of summary judgment

relevance.INP-01: Establishes that the mandatory-reporting duty is enforced criminally, not through private damages suits.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms the same rule applies to any person who has reason to believe a child is a victim.
relevance.INP-03: Notes the reporting duty runs to DCS or the appropriate law enforcement agency.
relevance.INP-06: Describes the immediate oral report to the hotline or law enforcement that the statute requires.
relevance.INP-07: Decided against a treating pediatrician, the paradigm medical-disclosure reporter.
relevance.INP-08: Applies the same universal reporting duty and its enforcement limits to any professional observer.

cases.case_name: Lake County Department of Child Services v. A.T.
cases.holding: The court reversed an order reinstating the wardship of a former CHINS ward, holding the juvenile court relinquished jurisdiction when it discharged her at age eighteen and could regain it only by the statutory methods.
cases.quote: Here, the juvenile court relinquished its jurisdiction over eighteen-year-old A.T. when it discharged her in August 2006.

relevance.OUT-04: The controlling Indiana decision on when juvenile court jurisdiction over a youth who has turned eighteen ends and how it may be reinstated.

cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of the mother's motion to dismiss, holding the dismissal sanction for an untimely CHINS fact-finding hearing cannot be used to collaterally attack an adjudication already entered.
cases.quote: The dismissal sanction of Indiana Code Section 31-34-11-1(d) for failure to timely conduct a CHINS factfinding hearing is not a mechanism to collaterally attack a CHINS adjudication.

relevance.DEC-05: Limits when a late fact-finding hearing defeats a filed CHINS petition.
relevance.OUT-05: Defines the point after which the statutory dismissal remedy is no longer available to a parent.

cases.holding: The court reversed the CHINS finding because the parents had cooperated fully and voluntarily obtained services, so there was insufficient evidence that the court's coercive intervention was necessary, noting an informal adjustment was available instead.
cases.quote: There is insufficient evidence that the coercive intervention of a court is necessary to protect E.K.

relevance.INP-05: Directly credits a family's own initiative in obtaining services as a reason not to open a court case.
relevance.INP-10: Holds that escalation to a formal court case is improper where cooperative parents have already obtained the needed services.
relevance.DEC-01: Provides the published basis for closing a case as unfounded or unnecessary where the family cooperates.
relevance.DEC-06: Expressly identifies the informal adjustment program as the appropriate alternative to a CHINS petition.
relevance.ACT-01: The clearest Indiana authority that voluntary participation in services defeats the need for a coercive service order.
relevance.OUT-05: Reversal of the CHINS finding requires dismissal where the coercion element fails.

cases.case_name: Siliven v. Indiana Department of Child Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for the Indiana DCS caseworkers on qualified immunity grounds, holding that the physician's opinion that the infant's injuries were non-accidental gave them probable cause, and therefore also reasonable suspicion, to remove the child without a court order.
cases.quote: The pertinent inquiry, then, is whether defendants had probable cause to believe that C.S.'s physical health would be seriously endangered if he was not immediately removed from his father's custody.

relevance.INP-03: Shows the joint agency and law-enforcement investigation posture that precedes an emergency removal in Indiana.
relevance.INP-12: States the federal constitutional standard Indiana caseworkers must satisfy before taking a child into protective custody without a court order.
relevance.DEC-02: Defines the evidentiary threshold an accepted investigation must reach before coercive action is constitutional.
relevance.DEC-04: The controlling Seventh Circuit decision on warrantless emergency removal by Indiana DCS workers.
relevance.FAIL-02: Sets out when a warrantless removal by Indiana caseworkers is, and is not, an unconstitutional seizure actionable under section 1983.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of qualified immunity to the Indiana DCS workers and the consulting physician, holding that a reasonable caseworker could have believed probable cause supported removing the children after a medical child abuse assessment, which also defeated the parents' Fourteenth Amendment familial-relations claims.
cases.quote: After conducting our own review of the factual record and evaluating each defendant and claim individually, as the law of qualified immunity demands, we reverse.

relevance.INP-07: Arises from a hospital's medical child abuse assessment that triggered the DCS report and removal.
relevance.INP-12: The most recent Seventh Circuit application of the emergency protective custody standard to Indiana DCS.
relevance.DEC-04: Shows how courts assess an emergency removal decision made when no judge was available to issue an order.
relevance.ACT-06: Concerns removal driven by a physician's assessment of the children's medical care and the parents' treatment decisions.
relevance.FAIL-02: Demonstrates the practical difficulty of a section 1983 wrongful-removal claim in Indiana given qualified immunity.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers violated the Fourth Amendment by entering a private school and interviewing a student without a warrant, consent, probable cause, or exigent circumstances, and violated the parents' right to familial relations by threatening removal, though the officials retained qualified immunity on some claims.
cases.quote: the amendment's prohibition against unreasonable searches and seizures protects against warrantless intrusions during civil as well as criminal investigations by the government

relevance.INP-08: The governing Seventh Circuit authority on interviewing a child at school without parental consent or a court order.
relevance.INP-12: Confirms that the Fourth Amendment constrains civil child-protection investigations, not only criminal ones.
relevance.DEC-02: Defines the constitutional limits on how an accepted report may be investigated through school-based interviews.
relevance.FAIL-02: Establishes that threats to remove children, and warrantless investigative seizures, can support section 1983 liability.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a child removed from his home on a false report of neglect stated Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment claims under section 1983, because a removal is reasonable only if supported by a court order, probable cause, or exigent circumstances.
cases.quote: governmental officials will not remove a child from his home without an investigation and pre-deprivation hearing resulting in a court order of removal, absent exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-03: Addresses removals carried out by officials acting on a referral that turned out to be false.
relevance.INP-12: The foundational Seventh Circuit statement of the constitutional prerequisites for taking a child into protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: Supplies the three-part test (court order, probable cause, or exigency) governing an emergency removal decision.
relevance.FAIL-02: The leading circuit authority under which an unlawful removal in Indiana is actionable under section 1983.

cases.case_name: Millspaugh v. County Department of Public Welfare of Wabash County
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that an Indiana caseworker has absolute immunity for initiating and prosecuting child-removal proceedings and for her testimony, but only qualified immunity for physically taking custody of the children.
cases.quote: Absolute immunity is appropriate when the social worker presents the case to a court, which can protect parents against misuse of public position.

relevance.DEC-04: Separates the court-facing acts that are absolutely immune from the physical removal that is only qualifiedly immune.
relevance.FAIL-02: Determines which Indiana caseworker conduct can actually be reached by a section 1983 damages claim for wrongful removal.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before terminating parental rights, striking down New York's fair-preponderance standard.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: The federal constitutional floor for the burden of proof in every Indiana termination of parental rights case.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not require appointed counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding, leaving the decision to the trial court on a case-by-case basis subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: Sets the federal constitutional baseline for appointed counsel in termination cases, above which Indiana's statutory right operates.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the reasonable efforts clause of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act creates no privately enforceable right and no implied cause of action, so beneficiaries cannot sue a state agency under section 1983 to enforce it.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.INP-09: Establishes that federal child-welfare plan requirements are enforced through federal administrative oversight rather than private suit.
relevance.FAIL-03: The controlling authority that federal reasonable-efforts noncompliance is remedied through funding oversight, not private litigation.
relevance.PMC-01: Explains why CFSR review and funding leverage, not lawsuits, are the operative enforcement tools for state plan failures.
relevance.PMC-02: Frames federal audit and funding penalties as the primary remedy for state child-welfare noncompliance.
relevance.PMC-03: Underscores why statutory review bodies matter given the absence of a private federal remedy.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes that public accountability work, not litigation, is the practical lever on federal plan compliance.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a state child-protection agency to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger, absent a custodial special relationship.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.OUT-06: The controlling federal rule limiting constitutional liability when a child known to the agency is killed or seriously injured at home.
relevance.FAIL-04: Explains why a child's death under agency supervision usually generates a state tort claim rather than a federal constitutional one.
relevance.PMC-04: Frames the accountability gap that fatality review commissions exist to address.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that removing a child from the custody of a fit natural mother because of the racial composition of her household violated equal protection, because private racial biases cannot be given effect by the law.
cases.quote: Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect.

relevance.FAIL-05: The controlling constitutional prohibition on race-based placement and custody decisions in child welfare.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected the Article I and anticommandeering challenges to the Indian Child Welfare Act and held that the individual petitioners and Texas lacked standing to press the equal protection and nondelegation challenges to the placement preferences, leaving ICWA intact.
cases.quote: Courts must adhere to the placement preferences absent “good cause” to depart from them.

relevance.INP-11: Confirms that ICWA's jurisdictional, procedural, and placement requirements remain binding on Indiana state courts.
relevance.FAIL-05: Leaves unresolved the equal protection challenge to ICWA's placement preferences for lack of standing, so no discrimination holding limits their application.

cases.case_name: Bester v. Lake County Office of Family & Children
cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of the father's parental rights, holding that several of the trial court's findings were misleading or unsupported and that the remaining findings did not clearly and convincingly establish that continuation of the parent-child relationship threatened the child's well-being.
cases.quote: The OFC bears the burden of proving these allegations by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.OUT-02: The controlling Indiana Supreme Court statement that the agency must prove each statutory element of Ind. Code 31-35-2-4(b)(2) by clear and convincing evidence, and the case later decisions cite for that standard.
relevance.OUT-01: Holds that an out-of-state home study declining to place the child with the father was irrelevant to whether the relationship threatened the child, keeping the reunification path open where the Interstate Compact does not govern.
relevance.FAIL-01: A leading reversal by the state's highest court of a termination judgment resting on findings that were misleading or unsupported by the evidence.

cases.case_name: Egly v. Blackford County Department of Public Welfare
cases.holding: The court granted transfer, vacated the Court of Appeals opinion and affirmed the termination, holding that the clear-and-convincing standard does not require proof that continued parental custody is wholly inadequate for the child's very survival, only that the child's emotional and physical development are threatened.
cases.quote: This includes situations not only where the child is in immediate danger of losing his life, but also where the child's emotional and physical development are threatened.

relevance.OUT-02: The foundational Indiana statement of what the heightened quantum of proof in a termination case actually requires, correcting the mistaken notion that the State must show the child's survival is at stake.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination of the mother's parental rights, holding the record clearly and convincingly supported the findings that the conditions leading to the children's removal would not be remedied and that termination served their need for permanency.
cases.quote: We engage in a two-step analysis to determine whether the conditions that led to the Children's placement outside the home will not be remedied.

relevance.OUT-02: The Indiana Supreme Court's leading modern statement of the two-step conditions-not-remedied inquiry and of permanency as a central best-interests consideration, the affirmance-side counterpart to Bester and In re V.A.

cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of the father's parental rights and remanded, holding the evidence did not clearly and convincingly support termination and observing that a permanent legal guardianship remained available if reunification proved unfeasible.
cases.quote: The evidence in a case involving the termination of a parent's constitutional right to parent his or her child must meet the heightened burden of clear and convincing.

relevance.OUT-02: The most recent Indiana Supreme Court reversal of a termination for failure to meet the heightened burden, and the court's reminder that termination is a last resort after all other reasonable efforts fail.
relevance.OUT-03: Directs courts and DCS to consider a permanent legal guardianship under Ind. Code 31-34-21-7.5 as the permanency option where neither reunification nor termination is viable.

cases.case_name: Hernandez ex rel. Hernandez v. Foster
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity on the claims arising from the child's initial removal but vacated summary judgment on the Fourth Amendment and substantive due process claims for continuing to withhold the child after probable cause had dissipated and on the claims that the caseworker coerced the parents into a safety plan.
cases.quote: The danger must be imminent, or put another way, the circumstances must be exigent.

relevance.INP-12: The Seventh Circuit's clearest holding that probable cause to take a child into protective custody must persist, and that general danger of future abuse is not enough to justify custody.
relevance.DEC-04: Establishes that the emergency-removal calculus is continuous: the decision to keep holding a child must be reassessed as new facts come in, not locked in for forty-eight hours.
relevance.ACT-01: Holds that a safety plan offered as the voluntary alternative to removal cannot be obtained through duress or threats of action the caseworker has no authority to take.
relevance.FAIL-02: The Seventh Circuit's leading decision denying qualified immunity to child-welfare workers, the necessary counterweight to Siliven, Mabes and Millspaugh in assessing a wrongful-removal claim.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that a child-protection caseworker violated the children's clearly established Fourth Amendment rights by conducting under-the-clothes body searches at their private school where the principal's consent to interview did not extend to searching the children's bodies.
cases.quote: it is a violation of a child's constitutional rights to conduct a search of a child at a private school without a warrant or probable cause, consent, or exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-08: The Seventh Circuit decision that actually denied immunity for a school-based child-protection search, giving INP-08 an enforceable rule rather than Doe v. Heck's immunity-protected warning alone.
relevance.INP-12: Confirms that a state child-abuse reporting statute does not itself authorize a warrantless search of a child and cannot substitute for the Fourth Amendment's requirements.
relevance.DEC-02: Fixes the limits of consent in an accepted investigation: permission to interview a child at school is not permission to examine the child's body.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court vacated summary judgment for the Indiana DCS caseworkers and remanded for trial, holding a jury must decide whether the parents' consent to a blood draw on their infant was voluntary or the product of a threatened CHINS filing and loss of the right to make her medical decisions.
cases.quote: Taking these facts together, the Jergers paint a picture of coercion, not “freely and voluntarily given” consent.

relevance.INP-07: Arises from a medical dispute over an epilepsy prescription that a social worker reported to DCS, the paradigm medical-disclosure intake in Indiana.
relevance.DEC-02: Holds that an accepted investigation may not be advanced by threatening a CHINS petition to extract consent to a medical test the agency has no order to compel.
relevance.ACT-06: The Indiana-origin Seventh Circuit authority on agency pressure to obtain medical testing or treatment over parents' contrary treatment decisions.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the Indiana-origin section 1983 case in which qualified immunity did NOT dispose of the claim, because the facts on coerced consent were genuinely disputed.

cases.case_name: F.T. v. Indiana Department of Child Services
cases.holding: The court vacated the parental participation decree entered against an alleged father, holding that paternity must be established first and that the statutory prerequisites, including a proper verified participation petition, must be met before a juvenile court has authority to order parental participation as part of a CHINS disposition.
cases.quote: Because the proper procedures were not followed here, the juvenile court did not have authority to order F.T.'s parental participation as part of its CHINS disposition.

relevance.ACT-05: The published Indiana authority on the procedural prerequisites for a court order directing and restraining a parent's conduct in a CHINS case, enforceable by contempt.
relevance.ACT-02: Holds that a court-ordered service and participation decree is void for want of authority unless the verified petition and hearing requirements of Ind. Code 31-34-16 are satisfied first.

cases.holding: The court reversed the entry of a second two-year protective order and remanded with instructions to vacate it, holding the record contained insufficient evidence that the respondent posed a present, credible threat to the petitioner's safety.
cases.quote: a trial court may issue a protective order only if presented with enough evidence that the respondent represents a present, credible threat to the petitioner's safety

relevance.ACT-05: The controlling Indiana Supreme Court statement of what a petitioner must prove under the Civil Protection Order Act before a court may restrain contact, the standard governing protective orders sought to keep an abuser away from a household with children.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the juvenile court's order ending all visits and phone contact between the mother and her child in a CHINS case, treating the order as effectively final and finding sufficient evidence that the contact endangered the child's emotional development.
cases.quote: While there is no statute specific to the CHINS context related to parenting time, we find the general family law statute on the issue to be instructive

relevance.ACT-05: The published Indiana decision on a CHINS no-contact order, importing the Ind. Code 31-17-4-2 endangerment finding as the predicate before a juvenile court may cut off a parent's contact.
relevance.OUT-04: Marks the end point of a CHINS wardship at age eighteen and identifies the Collaborative Care program, Ind. Code 31-28-5.8, as the successor mechanism for services to an older youth.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its majority opinion text read; each quote was programmatically verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after whitespace and curly-quote normalization.

No unpublished memorandum decisions are used. The key_cases already present in the IN node files are almost entirely Indiana Court of Appeals memorandum decisions issued under App. R. 65(D) (not regarded as precedent) with synthetic citations; none of them survived verification and none are carried forward.

Indiana is a universal mandatory-reporting state (Ind. Code 31-33-5-1). No published Indiana appellate decision was found construing the reporter-immunity statute, Ind. Code 31-33-6-1 to -3, in a defendant's favor. The closest published authorities are C.T. v. Gammon (no private right of action for failure to report), John Doe #1 (no private remedy for the agency's breach of reporter anonymity) and Gresk v. Demetris (anti-SLAPP does not shield a reporting physician from a malpractice suit about her care).

ACT-05 is no longer a single-case node. Three published authorities were added in this pass: S.H. v. D.W. (Ind. 2020) for the Civil Protection Order Act standard, F.T. (Ind. Ct. App. 2010) for the procedural prerequisites to a parental participation decree, and In re E.W. (Ind. Ct. App. 2015) for a CHINS order terminating all parent-child contact. In re Am.K., referenced in the prior pass, was not retrieved and is not relied on.

Extended foster care / jurisdiction past 18 (OUT-04) remains thin in published Indiana case law. Lake County DCS v. A.T. is the controlling published decision on when juvenile court jurisdiction over an eighteen-year-old former CHINS ward ends. In re E.W. identifies the Collaborative Care statute, Ind. Code 31-28-5.8, but no retrieved published Indiana decision construes it. Because the node otherwise rests on federal program law, Suter v. Artist M. is mapped as the federal standard: Collaborative Care is funded through the Title IV-E state plan and Suter holds IV-E plan obligations are enforced through federal oversight, not a youth's private suit.

No published Indiana appellate decision was found applying ICWA's active-efforts or qualified-expert-witness requirements in a modern CHINS or termination case. D.S. (Ind. 1991) remains the state's statement that ICWA's jurisdictional and beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standards control, and it rejects the 'existing Indian family' exception. Haaland v. Brackeen (2023) confirms ICWA's continued force but did not reach the equal protection challenge to the placement preferences. Practitioners should also check the 2016 federal ICWA regulations, 25 C.F.R. Part 23, which post-date the Indiana cases.

Indiana has no reported appellate decision squarely on due-process challenges to a substantiated finding and the DCS Child Protection Index (Ind. Code 31-33-26); administrative review runs through DCS under 465 IAC 3-3 and AOPA. Indiana DCS v. A.B. supplies the AOPA judicial-review standards the courts apply to DCS decisions. A lawyer should not assume the out-of-state central-registry due process line (e.g., Valmonte) has been adopted in Indiana.

Section 1983 wrongful-removal claims from Indiana are governed by the Seventh Circuit. Brokaw states the rule. FAIL-02 is now balanced: Siliven, Mabes and Millspaugh show how readily qualified immunity defeats such claims, while Hernandez and Jerger show the circumstances in which it does not. Millspaugh (an Indiana case) fixes the absolute/qualified immunity line: absolute for presenting the case to the court and testifying, qualified only for physically taking custody.

FAIL-03 (federal compliance failure) and the PMC oversight nodes have no on-point Indiana case law. They are anchored to the federal standard: Suter v. Artist M. holds the Title IV-E reasonable-efforts clause is not privately enforceable, so CFSR, Single Audit and funding penalties are the operative mechanisms. PMC-03 (Citizen Review Panels, 42 U.S.C. 5106a(c)) and PMC-06 (analysis layer) have no judicial construction at all; the cases mapped to them supply the surrounding Indiana records and oversight law rather than a holding on the node itself.

FAIL-05 (discrimination/retaliation) has no reported Indiana child-welfare discrimination decision. Palmore v. Sidoti supplies the federal equal protection rule against race-based placement; Gresk v. Demetris supplies Indiana's anti-SLAPP framework for retaliatory-suit claims.

Case names are given as the reporters style them; the cluster_id and URL identify the CourtListener record, whose caption often differs. In re G.Y. appears as 'R.Y. v. Indiana Department of Child Services'; In re K.B. as 'Lay v. Department of Child Services'; In re G.R. as 'Leonelli v. Noble County Department of Child Services'; In re G.P. as 'J.A. v. Indiana Department of Child Services'; In re Bi.B. as 'Termination: VG v. Indiana Department of Child Services'; In re K.T.K. as 'R.C. v. Indiana Department of Child Services'; In re V.A. and In re E.W. under their long CHINS/termination captions; Jerger v. Blaize as 'Lelah Jerger v. Shannon Blaize'.

The CourtListener cluster for S.H. v. D.W. carries no reporter citation, so the entry uses slip form, 'No. 19S-PO-118 (Ind. Jan. 31, 2020)'. The opinion text retrieved is the majority by Justice Slaughter; Justice Goff's dissent (joined by Justice Massa) was not used.

In re I.B. holds the statutory right to counsel extends through appeal, but on its facts the court affirmed the refusal to appoint appellate counsel because trial counsel had no basis for an appeal; do not cite it for an automatic right to appointed appellate counsel.

In re S.A. is an opinion on rehearing; the original opinion is reported at 15 N.E.3d 602 (Ind. Ct. App. 2014). In re J.S. and In re S.A. cut in different directions on the sixty-day fact-finding deadline and should be read together.

No published Indiana authority was found on missing children from foster care, sibling-placement preference as a distinct doctrine, or discrimination in foster-parent licensing; those aspects of ACT-03, ACT-04 and FAIL-05 rest on statute and the federal standards cited here.

Added Bester v. Lake County Office of Family & Children, 839 N.E.2d 143 (Ind. 2005) for OUT-02, OUT-01 and FAIL-01: it is the controlling Indiana Supreme Court statement that the agency bears the clear-and-convincing burden on each element of Ind. Code 31-35-2-4(b)(2), the case In re G.Y., In re K.E. and In re Bi.B. all cite for the standard, and it reverses a termination on unsupported findings while holding the Interstate Compact irrelevant to placement with a parent.

Added Egly v. Blackford County Department of Public Welfare, 592 N.E.2d 1232 (Ind. 1992) for OUT-02: the foundational Indiana decision fixing what the heightened quantum of proof actually requires, rejecting the notion that the State must show continued parental custody is wholly inadequate for the child's very survival. Note the disposition: the court granted transfer and AFFIRMED the termination; it is authority on the standard, not a reversal.

Added In re K.T.K., 989 N.E.2d 1225 (Ind. 2013) (cluster 7167202) for OUT-02: the Indiana Supreme Court's leading modern statement of the two-step conditions-not-remedied inquiry and of permanency as a central best-interests factor. It is NOT mapped to DEC-03 as the verifier suggested: K.T.K. is a termination sufficiency case and contains no holding on a substantiated or founded agency finding. Its well-known 'need not wait until the child is irreversibly harmed' language is a quotation of In re C.M., 675 N.E.2d 1134 (Ind. Ct. App. 1997), not the supreme court's own sentence, so it was not used as the quote.

Added In re V.A., 51 N.E.3d 1140 (Ind. 2016) for OUT-02 and OUT-03: the most recent Indiana Supreme Court reversal of a termination for failure to meet the heightened burden, and the court's direction that a permanent legal guardianship under Ind. Code 31-34-21-7.5 be considered where neither reunification nor termination is viable.

Added Hernandez ex rel. Hernandez v. Foster, 657 F.3d 463 (7th Cir. 2011) for INP-12, DEC-04, ACT-01 and FAIL-02: the circuit's leading decision denying qualified immunity to child-welfare workers, holding that probable cause to hold a child must persist and dissipates with new facts, that general danger of future abuse is not exigency, and that a safety plan cannot be extracted by duress.

Added Michael C. v. Gresbach, 526 F.3d 1008 (7th Cir. 2008) for INP-08, INP-12 and DEC-02: it affirms the DENIAL of qualified immunity for a caseworker's warrantless under-the-clothes search of children at a private school, giving INP-08 an enforceable rule rather than Doe v. Heck's immunity-protected warning alone.

Added Jerger v. Blaize, 41 F.4th 910 (7th Cir. 2022) for ACT-06, INP-07, DEC-02 and FAIL-02: the Indiana-origin Seventh Circuit decision vacating summary judgment for DCS workers where a jury could find the parents' consent to a blood draw on their epileptic infant was coerced by a threatened CHINS filing. This replaces the misread In re A.M.-K. as the brief's Indiana medical-decision authority.

Added F.T. v. Indiana Department of Child Services, 934 N.E.2d 1253 (Ind. Ct. App. 2010) for ACT-05 and ACT-02: the published Indiana decision holding a juvenile court is without authority to enter a parental participation decree unless paternity is established and the verified-petition and hearing prerequisites of Ind. Code 31-34-16 are met.

Added S.H. v. D.W., No. 19S-PO-118 (Ind. Jan. 31, 2020) for ACT-05: the Indiana Supreme Court's controlling statement that a protective order under the Civil Protection Order Act requires evidence of a present, credible threat to the petitioner's safety, the standard governing an order to remove or restrain an abuser rather than the child.

Added In re E.W., 26 N.E.3d 1006 (Ind. Ct. App. 2015) for ACT-05 and OUT-04: it supplies the endangerment predicate a juvenile court must find before cutting off a parent's contact in a CHINS case, and it identifies the Collaborative Care program for older youth. Its Collaborative Care discussion is in a footnote and is descriptive, not a holding.
Added Suter v. Artist M. to OUT-04 as the federal standard, per instruction, because no published Indiana decision beyond Lake County DCS v. A.T. was located on extended foster care or aging out.

All seven authorities the verifier named as missing were located on CourtListener, retrieved, read and confirmed real and on point. None had to be dropped as unverifiable. Two corrections to the verifier's descriptions: Bester was decided 2005-12-20 (not earlier in 2005), and Hernandez affirmed qualified immunity on the INITIAL removal while denying it only on the continued-withholding and safety-plan claims, so it should not be cited for the proposition that the removal itself lacked exigency.

Rebalancing to honor the 2-6 cases per node standard: OUT-02 previously carried six cases and four of the named missing authorities belong there, which would have produced ten. OUT-02 now holds the six that cover distinct doctrinal ground (Santosky, Lassiter, Bester, Egly, K.T.K., V.A.). No case was removed from the brief; the four displaced mappings were moved to the nodes where they are independently on point: In re Bi.B. to OUT-05 (dismissal required when DCS fails to prove a pleaded element), In re K.E. to OUT-01 (incarcerated parent who maintains contact and completes programs), In re E.M. and In re I.B. to ACT-02 (late compliance with court-ordered services; scope of the statutory right to counsel). Doe v. Heck was likewise moved off FAIL-02, where Hernandez and Jerger now carry the denial-of-immunity side, and retains its INP-08, INP-12 and DEC-02 mappings.

Case count is 47, above the 20-40 target, because the instruction to leave all previously verified entries unchanged was followed while adding the ten authorities needed to close the named gaps and the sub-2 nodes.

Missing (for a later pass): In re C.G., 954 N.E.2d 910 (Ind. 2011) — the Indiana Supreme Court source of the controlling 'involuntary termination of parental rights is an extreme measure that is designed to be used as a last resort when all other reasonable efforts have failed' principle. Confirmed to exist because In re V.A. quotes and cites it at 916 in the text I retrieved. Its absence is conspicuous: the brief relies on V.A.'s last-resort language for OUT-02 while omitting the case that actually states it.

Missing (for a later pass): In re I.A., 934 N.E.2d 1127 (Ind. 2010) — Indiana Supreme Court authority on termination sufficiency and the conditions-not-remedied inquiry. Confirmed to exist because In re K.T.K. cites it at 1134 in the text I retrieved. It is the decision K.T.K. builds its two-step analysis on, and OUT-02 currently cites the derivative without the source.

Missing (for a later pass): Matter of Miedl, 425 N.E.2d 137 (Ind. 1981) — the Indiana Supreme Court decision whose 'wholly inadequate for their very survival' sentence Egly expressly held to be dicta. Confirmed to exist because Egly quotes and cites it at 141. Any brief that relies on Egly for the quantum of proof should cite Miedl alongside it, since practitioners and lower courts still encounter the Miedl formulation and need the Egly correction paired with its source.

Missing (for a later pass): In re S.A., 15 N.E.3d 602 (Ind. Ct. App. 2014) — on the Ind. Code 31-34-11-1 sixty-day CHINS fact-finding deadline and the dismissal sanction. The brief's own notes state that S.A. and In re J.S. cut in different directions and must be read together, and that S.A. has an opinion on rehearing — yet S.A. appears nowhere in the case list or node_map. DEC-05 and OUT-05 currently present only the J.S. side of a split, which is the kind of one-sided presentation that gets a brief distinguished.

Missing (for a later pass): Ind. Code 31-33-6-1 to -3 reporter immunity — no published Indiana appellate construction was located, which the brief correctly notes. Flagging it here as a genuine gap rather than an omission: INP-01, INP-02 and INP-06 currently tell a reporter only what protections do NOT exist (no private right of action, no enforceable anonymity, no anti-SLAPP shield) without any authority on the immunity that does. Counsel advising a mandated reporter should be warned the brief is one-sided on this point.
